title: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM)
hook: Wreck an image into pure static one tiny step at a time, then train a network to undo it. Run the undo from random noise and you get a brand-new image.
key_points: Forward process gradually adds Gaussian noise until an image becomes pure static.
A network learns to reverse one denoising step at a time.
Sampling starts from random noise and denoises down to a clean image.
Achieves high sample quality with stable training, unlike many GANs.
Became the foundation for modern image generators.
content_html: Ho, Jain, and Abbeel showed how to generate high-quality images by learning to reverse a noising process. You take a clean image, add a little noise over and over until it's indistinguishable from static, then train a network to walk that back step by step. Generating a new image means starting from pure noise and denoising. The approach delivered excellent quality with notably stable training.
extra_html:
How it works

There are two processes. The forward (fixed, not learned) process slowly corrupts a training image by adding small amounts of Gaussian noise across many steps. The reverse process is what the network learns: at each step it predicts the noise that was added, so it can subtract a bit of it and produce a slightly cleaner image. To sample, you begin with random noise and apply this learned denoiser repeatedly, gradually revealing a coherent image. The denoiser is typically a U-Net.

Why it matters

Diffusion models gave generation a training recipe that is far more stable than the adversarial game GANs play, while reaching competitive or better image quality. This paper is the technical backbone of the text-to-image systems that followed, including latent diffusion and the consumer tools built on it. The trade-off is speed: sampling takes many steps, which later work has worked hard to reduce.

related.title: High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion (Stable Diffusion)
related.hook: Running diffusion on raw pixels is brutally expensive. Do it in a compressed latent space instead, and high-res text-to-image becomes cheap enough to run on a consumer GPU.

related.title: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)
related.hook: Pit two networks against each other — a forger making fakes and a detective catching them — and the forger gets so good its fakes look real.

related.title: Classifier-Free Guidance
related.hook: Want a diffusion model to follow your prompt more closely? Blend its prompt-aware and prompt-blind predictions — no extra classifier required. That's the guidance-scale slider.

prereqs.title: How Neural Networks Learn: Backpropagation
prereqs.hook: A neural net learns by asking, for every weight, 'how much did you contribute to my mistake?' Backprop answers all of them at once.

flashcards.prompt: In DDPM, which process is fixed (not learned) and which does the network learn?

choices.text: The forward noising process is fixed; the reverse denoising process is learned
The forward process is learned; the reverse process is fixed

flashcards.explanation_html: The forward process slowly adds Gaussian noise (fixed). The network learns the reverse: predicting the noise so it can subtract a bit each step.

flashcards.prompt: How does DDPM generate a brand-new image at sampling time?
flashcards.back_html: It starts from pure random noise and applies the learned denoiser repeatedly, gradually revealing a coherent image.

flashcards.prompt: What advantage does diffusion training have over GANs, and what's the trade-off?
flashcards.back_html: Training is far more stable than the adversarial game GANs play, with competitive quality — but sampling is slow, taking many steps.
